title: Analytical photogrammetry and the collinearity equations
institutions: Ballistic Research Laboratories, Aberdeen Proving Ground
summary: The ray geometry once embodied in instruments was written as equations and solved numerically on electronic computers.
context: Ballistic missile tracking in the 1950s demanded higher accuracy than analog instruments could provide. At the US Army's Ballistic Research Laboratories, Schmid formulated a general least-squares treatment of photogrammetric triangulation, with rigorous error propagation.
contribution: The collinearity equations — image point, projection centre and object point on one line — became the universal observation model, solved by iterative least squares.
technicalExplanation: x = x₀ − c·[r₁₁(X−X₀)+r₂₁(Y−Y₀)+r₃₁(Z−Z₀)] / [r₁₃(X−X₀)+r₂₃(Y−Y₀)+r₃₃(Z−Z₀)], and similarly for y. Unknowns are exterior orientation (X₀,Y₀,Z₀, R), interior orientation (c, x₀, y₀) and object coordinates; the equations are linearised and solved by Gauss–Newton.
historicalSignificance: Separated photogrammetry from its instruments. Any camera, any geometry and any number of images could be handled, provided computation was available.
limitations: Computationally heavy for 1950s machines; required good initial values.

dates.adoption: Satellite geodesy and military applications 1960s; civil mapping 1970s

uncertainty: The collinearity condition itself is classical; the attribution concerns its systematic use as a computational model.

title: Bundle adjustment
institutions: RCA Missile Test Project, Patrick Air Force Base
summary: Simultaneous least-squares estimation of all camera orientations and all object points from all image observations.
context: Brown's 1958 technical report gave a general solution to multi-station analytical triangulation, exploiting the sparse block structure of the normal equations so the problem became tractable.
contribution: Treated each image as a bundle of rays and adjusted all bundles jointly so that corresponding rays meet optimally, minimising reprojection error.
technicalExplanation: Minimise Σᵢⱼ ‖xᵢⱼ − π(Pᵢ, Xⱼ)‖² over cameras Pᵢ and points Xⱼ. The normal-equation matrix has a sparse arrowhead structure; eliminating points via the Schur complement leaves a reduced camera system.
historicalSignificance: The most enduring algorithm in this atlas. It is the final stage of COLMAP and every SfM system, the refinement step behind 3DGS initialisation, and the benchmark against which feed-forward methods are compared.
limitations: Non-convex; requires good initialisation and outlier removal; datum (gauge) must be defined.

dates.publication: RCA Data Reduction Technical Report No. 43, 1958
dates.improvements: Self-calibration (1971); sparse solvers; robust kernels; Triggs et al. synthesis (1999)

uncertainty: Parallel developments (Schmid; Ackermann's group) mean 'invention' is shared; Brown's report is the commonly cited origin of the bundle method.

title: The analytical plotter
summary: A stereo viewer whose image carriages are driven by a computer solving the collinearity equations in real time.
context: Helava proposed the principle in 1957. Early systems were built in the early 1960s for military mapping; the technology became mainstream after the 1976 ISP congress in Helsinki, where several manufacturers presented analytical plotters.
contribution: Replaced optical–mechanical ray reconstruction with computation, removing instrument constraints on camera type, focal length and geometry.
technicalExplanation: The operator moves in object space (X,Y,Z); the computer projects the position into both images via collinearity and positions the plates accordingly, keeping the floating mark on the model.
historicalSignificance: The bridge between analog and digital photogrammetry: still human stereo perception, but computational geometry.
limitations: Costly; still analog film; measurement remained manual.

title: The digital terrain model
summary: Terrain represented as a numerical array of heights rather than as drawn contours.
context: Working on highway engineering at MIT, Miller and Laflamme proposed sampling terrain heights from photogrammetric stereo models and storing them for computer analysis.
contribution: Introduced terrain as data — a representation computers could analyse (earthworks, slopes) and later generate automatically.
technicalExplanation: A DTM/DEM stores heights on a regular grid or triangulated irregular network (TIN). Contours, slope, visibility and orthophotos are derived products.
historicalSignificance: The first widely adopted digital 3D representation derived from images; the ancestor of dense point clouds and meshes.
limitations: 2.5D — one height per planimetric position; overhangs and vertical structure cannot be represented.

dates.improvements: Automated DEMs by image matching (1980s–); SRTM global DEM (2000); LiDAR DEMs

title: Machine perception of three-dimensional solids
summary: A computer recovered the 3D shape and pose of polyhedral objects from a single photograph — an origin point of computer vision.
context: Roberts' doctoral thesis used edge detection, homogeneous coordinates and model matching to interpret 'blocks world' scenes.
contribution: Introduced the goal of automatic scene interpretation and brought projective (homogeneous) camera matrices into computing.
technicalExplanation: Edges are extracted, grouped into polygons, and matched to a library of polyhedral models; a 4×4 homogeneous transformation and projection recovers model pose.
historicalSignificance: Marks the start of the computer-vision lineage, which grew largely independently from photogrammetry until their convergence around 2000–2010.
limitations: Restricted to idealised polyhedral scenes.

title: Lens distortion models and self-calibration
summary: Camera interior orientation and lens distortion estimated as unknowns within the bundle adjustment itself.
context: Building on Conrady's (1919) treatment of decentred lenses, Brown published the decentring distortion model (1966) and the self-calibrating bundle adjustment for close-range cameras (1971).
contribution: Made non-metric and close-range cameras usable for precise measurement; the Brown–Conrady model is still the default distortion model in OpenCV and COLMAP.
technicalExplanation: Radial distortion Δr = k₁r³ + k₂r⁵ + k₃r⁷ and decentring terms p₁, p₂ are added to the collinearity equations; principal distance, principal point and distortion coefficients are estimated with the orientations from a strong multi-image network.
historicalSignificance: Calibration is the junction where photogrammetry, computer vision and neural rendering meet: NeRF and 3DGS still assume an undistorted pinhole obtained this way.
limitations: Parameter correlations with weak geometry; models fail for fisheye and rolling-shutter cameras without extension.

dates.improvements: Tsai (1987), Zhang (2000) calibration in computer vision

title: Direct Linear Transformation and camera calibration
summary: A linear model relating image and object coordinates, solvable without initial values; later the standard computer-vision camera matrix.
context: Abdel-Aziz and Karara proposed the DLT for close-range photogrammetry with non-metric cameras (1971). Computer vision adopted the same linear 3×4 camera matrix; Tsai (1987) and Zhang (2000, planar checkerboard) produced the calibration methods most widely used in vision and robotics.
contribution: Gave a closed-form initialisation for camera parameters and made calibration accessible to non-specialists.
technicalExplanation: x ≃ P X with P a 3×4 matrix (11 DOF), estimated linearly from ≥6 control points; P decomposes into K[R|t]. Zhang's method estimates K from homographies of a planar target seen in several views, then refines non-linearly.
historicalSignificance: A clear case of the same mathematics living in both communities under different names.
limitations: Linear estimation ignores distortion and is not statistically optimal; refined by bundle adjustment.

title: Aerial triangulation in production
summary: Block adjustment software made analytical triangulation of thousands of aerial images routine in mapping agencies.
context: Ackermann's group in Stuttgart developed block adjustment with independent models (PAT-M) and bundle block adjustment (PAT-B), widely used in production from the 1970s. Research on reliability (Baarda's data snooping, 1968) and on self-calibration made the results statistically controlled.
contribution: Reduced ground control requirements and turned triangulation into a computational service with statistically tested quality.
technicalExplanation: Blocks of overlapping strips are adjusted with tie points, sparse ground control and later GPS-observed projection centres. Gross-error detection tests standardised residuals.
historicalSignificance: Established the large-scale, quality-controlled estimation practice that computer vision would rediscover for internet photo collections.
limitations: Tie points still measured manually or semi-automatically until the 1990s.
uncertainty: Software and publication dates vary across versions.

title: Computational theory of stereo vision
summary: Stereo correspondence formulated as a computational problem with explicit constraints — uniqueness, continuity, compatibility.
context: Marr and Poggio proposed a cooperative algorithm for random-dot stereograms (1976) and a coarse-to-fine theory (1979). Marr's Vision (1982) framed perception as a sequence of representations.
contribution: Defined the matching problem that dense stereo algorithms solve: find disparities subject to smoothness and uniqueness priors.
technicalExplanation: Correspondences are constrained by the epipolar line, a smoothness prior on disparity and a one-to-one matching assumption; ambiguity is resolved by cooperative or coarse-to-fine computation.
historicalSignificance: Inspired decades of stereo research leading to global energy minimisation, SGM and learned stereo.
limitations: Biologically motivated, not metrically rigorous.

title: The essential matrix and the eight-point algorithm
summary: A linear algorithm for the relative orientation of two calibrated views from eight correspondences.
context: Published in Nature, the paper encoded the coplanarity condition — known to photogrammetrists since the early 20th century — as a single 3×3 matrix.
contribution: Gave computer vision a compact algebraic formulation of two-view geometry and a linear solution.
technicalExplanation: For normalised image points x, x′: x′ᵀ E x = 0 with E = [t]ₓR. Eight correspondences give a linear system for E; decomposition yields R and t up to scale. The uncalibrated analogue is the fundamental matrix F.
historicalSignificance: A canonical example of parallel rediscovery: photogrammetric relative orientation reframed as linear algebra, which made it easy to embed in automatic pipelines.
limitations: Numerically sensitive without normalisation (Hartley, 1997); not minimal.

title: RANSAC — random sample consensus
summary: Robust model fitting by repeatedly fitting minimal samples and keeping the hypothesis with the most inliers.
context: Developed for the 'location determination problem' (camera resection from landmarks) in automated cartography, the paper solved P3P inside a hypothesise-and-verify loop.
contribution: Made automatic estimation possible in the presence of many wrong correspondences — the precondition for automated matching pipelines.
technicalExplanation: Draw a minimal sample (e.g. 3 points for P3P, 5 for relative pose), compute the model, count observations within a threshold; repeat N times where N depends on the inlier ratio and confidence.
historicalSignificance: Photogrammetry handled blunders by statistical testing after adjustment; RANSAC tolerated outlier rates far beyond what least squares can handle, enabling automatic feature matching.
limitations: Threshold-dependent; cost grows rapidly with low inlier ratios.

title: Volume rendering and its optical model
summary: Rendering participating media by integrating emission and absorption along rays — the image-formation model NeRF would later invert.
context: Kajiya and Von Herzen (1984) ray-traced volume densities; Levoy (1988) and Drebin et al. (1988) applied volume rendering to medical data; Max (1995) systematised the optical models.
contribution: Provided a differentiable, continuous model of how density and colour along a ray produce a pixel.
technicalExplanation: C = ∫ T(t) σ(t) c(t) dt with transmittance T(t) = exp(−∫σ). Discretised as alpha compositing: C = Σ Tᵢ αᵢ cᵢ.
historicalSignificance: Computer graphics, not photogrammetry, provided the forward model on which neural radiance fields and, in rasterised form, Gaussian splatting are built.
limitations: Forward rendering only; no reconstruction until differentiable optimisation.

title: Digital image matching
summary: Automatic determination of corresponding points by correlating image intensities.
context: Hobrough built electronic correlators for automatic stereo (late 1950s). With digitised imagery in the 1980s, area-based matching was formulated as least-squares estimation (Ackermann 1984; Gruen 1985), achieving sub-pixel precision with quality measures.
contribution: Replaced the human stereo operator for point transfer and DEM generation; least-squares matching integrated matching into the photogrammetric error theory.
technicalExplanation: Least-squares matching estimates an affine geometric and linear radiometric transformation between a template and search window by minimising grey-value differences; geometric constraints (epipolar, collinearity) can be added.
historicalSignificance: The core of automatic DEM generation and automatic aerial triangulation in the 1990s.
limitations: Requires good approximations; fails on low texture, occlusions and wide baselines.
uncertainty: Early correlator dates vary across sources.

title: Interest operators and corner detection
summary: Detectors that select distinctive, precisely localisable points suitable for automatic matching.
context: Moravec's operator (late 1970s) served robot navigation. Förstner and Gülch (1987) derived a detector from the precision of least-squares matching; Harris and Stephens (1988) proposed the closely related corner detector that became standard in vision.
contribution: Shifted matching from dense correlation to sparse, well-conditioned features — the idea that SIFT and SfM pipelines build on.
technicalExplanation: Both use the structure tensor M = Σ ∇I ∇Iᵀ in a window; corners have two large eigenvalues. Förstner relates M to the covariance of the point's position; Harris scores det(M) − k·trace(M)².
historicalSignificance: A direct photogrammetry/vision convergence: the same eigenvalue analysis of local image structure, motivated by precision in one community and by repeatability in the other.
limitations: Not invariant to scale; descriptors still required.

title: Surface extraction and volumetric fusion
summary: Methods to turn sampled volumes and range images into watertight triangle meshes.
context: Marching cubes (1987) extracted iso-surfaces from medical volumes. Curless and Levoy (1996) fused many range scans into a signed-distance volume, the method behind the Digital Michelangelo Project.
contribution: Established implicit signed-distance fields and iso-surface extraction as a route from measurements to meshes.
technicalExplanation: Each range image contributes weighted signed distances to voxels along lines of sight; the zero level set of the averaged field is extracted with marching cubes.
historicalSignificance: The template for KinectFusion's TSDF (2011) and for extracting surfaces from neural SDFs (NeuS, 2021).
limitations: Memory grows cubically; resolution limited by voxel size.

title: Digital (softcopy) photogrammetry
summary: Scanned and later natively digital images processed on computer workstations, with automatic matching replacing optical instruments.
context: Digital photogrammetric workstations were presented at the 1988 ISPRS congress in Kyoto and became production systems during the 1990s, using scanned film. Large-format digital aerial cameras (e.g. Leica ADS40 and Z/I DMC around 2000–2001; Vexcel UltraCam 2003) completed the transition.
contribution: Automated interior orientation, tie-point extraction, DEM generation and orthophoto production.
technicalExplanation: Epipolar resampling, image pyramids, least-squares and feature-based matching, automatic aerial triangulation, orthorectification using DEMs.
historicalSignificance: Ended the era of the optical–mechanical instrument. The workflow — orient, match, densify, orthorectify — is recognisable inside modern SfM–MVS software.
limitations: Proprietary, expensive, designed for vertical aerial blocks with metric cameras.
uncertainty: Which system was 'first' depends on definitions; several prototypes existed in the mid-1980s.

title: GPS/INS integration and direct georeferencing
summary: Satellite positioning and inertial navigation measured camera position and orientation directly in flight.
context: GPS-supported aerial triangulation (late 1980s) reduced ground control. Integrated GPS/INS (early 1990s) provided full exterior orientation, essential for line scanners and airborne LiDAR.
contribution: Made exterior orientation an observation rather than only an unknown, and enabled sensors without frame geometry.
technicalExplanation: Kalman filtering fuses GNSS positions and IMU accelerations and rates; lever-arm and boresight calibration relate the navigation frame to the camera frame. Observed poses enter bundle adjustment as weighted observations.
historicalSignificance: Underpins airborne LiDAR, mobile mapping and today's UAV photogrammetry; in vision the analogue is visual–inertial odometry.
limitations: Boresight misalignment and GNSS outages; IMU drift.

title: Projective and multiple-view geometry
summary: Reconstruction from uncalibrated images, up to a projective ambiguity, and its upgrade to metric structure.
context: In 1992 Faugeras and Hartley independently showed what can be reconstructed from uncalibrated views. Tomasi and Kanade introduced factorisation for affine cameras (1992); trifocal tensors and auto-calibration followed. Hartley and Zisserman's Multiple View Geometry (2000) consolidated the field.
contribution: A complete algebraic theory of two-, three- and N-view geometry that does not require calibrated cameras — essential for internet photographs.
technicalExplanation: From F alone cameras are recovered up to a 4×4 homography H; constraints on K (auto-calibration, e.g. via the absolute conic) upgrade to metric. Factorisation stacks image tracks into a rank-3 measurement matrix decomposed by SVD.
historicalSignificance: Gave computer vision the tools to initialise reconstruction from unknown cameras, a step photogrammetry had avoided by calibrating first.
limitations: Projective algebra ignores noise models; final accuracy still needs bundle adjustment.

title: Image-based modelling and rendering
summary: Rendering new views directly from captured images, with or without explicit geometry.
context: At SIGGRAPH 1996 three influential papers appeared: Light Field Rendering, The Lumigraph, and Façade (photogrammetric modelling of architecture plus view-dependent texture mapping).
contribution: Reframed the goal from measuring geometry to reproducing appearance — novel-view synthesis — and showed that appearance can be represented as a sampled function of rays.
technicalExplanation: The 4D light field L(u,v,s,t) parameterises rays between two planes; new views are slices of it. Façade fitted parametric architectural primitives to photographs by minimising reprojection error, then used view-dependent texture.
historicalSignificance: The intellectual ancestor of neural radiance fields: NeRF is evaluated, like these methods, by how well it renders held-out views.
limitations: Dense sampling required (light fields); manual modelling (Façade).

title: Multi-camera capture of dynamic scenes
summary: Domes of synchronised cameras reconstructed moving people and events frame by frame.
context: CMU's Virtualized Reality project (1997) used a dome of video cameras to reconstruct dynamic events. The CMU Panoptic Studio (2015) scaled to hundreds of synchronised cameras for social motion capture.
contribution: Introduced time as a dimension of image-based reconstruction and the synchronised multi-view rig as its instrument.
technicalExplanation: Per-frame multi-baseline stereo and volumetric merging across calibrated, genlocked cameras; later with keypoint detection and 3D trajectory reconstruction.
historicalSignificance: The capture paradigm behind datasets used to train and evaluate dynamic NeRF and 4D Gaussian methods.
limitations: Frame-independent reconstruction lacked temporal coherence; heavy infrastructure.

title: Bundle Adjustment — A Modern Synthesis
summary: A survey that brought photogrammetric bundle adjustment, its sparsity and its gauge theory into computer vision.
context: Presented at the 1999 Vision Algorithms workshop (ICCV), the paper explicitly acknowledged the photogrammetric literature and explained sparse solvers, robust cost functions and gauge freedom to vision researchers.
contribution: Made bundle adjustment the accepted final step of vision reconstruction and fostered its efficient implementation.
technicalExplanation: Levenberg–Marquardt with Schur complement on the camera block, robust M-estimators, covariance and gauge analysis, network design.
historicalSignificance: The clearest bridge text between the two lineages; open-source solvers (SBA 2009, Ceres Solver) followed.

dates.improvements: SBA, Ceres, GPU and distributed BA
